must_allow.text: A lipid panel measures total cholesterol, LDL, HDL and triglycerides in a sample of blood.
Hemoglobin A1c reflects average blood glucose over roughly the past two to three months.
Fasting for 8 to 12 hours before a lipid or glucose test matters because a recent meal can raise triglycerides and glucose.
A reference range is the span of values found in about 95% of a healthy comparison group, so some healthy people fall outside it.
TSH stands for thyroid-stimulating hormone, which the pituitary gland releases to tell the thyroid how much hormone to make.
Creatinine is a waste product from muscle that the kidneys filter out of the blood.
eGFR is an estimate, calculated from creatinine, age and sex, of how much blood the kidneys filter each minute.
Glucose is usually reported in mg/dL in the United States and in mmol/L in many other countries.
Ferritin is a protein that stores iron, and the test gives an indirect picture of the body's iron stores.
A complete blood count reports red cells, white cells and platelets, along with hemoglobin and hematocrit.
Vitamin D is usually measured as 25-hydroxyvitamin D and reported in ng/mL or nmol/L, while supplement labels list amounts in IU (international units).
The INR is a standardized way of reporting how long blood takes to clot.
ALT and AST are enzymes found mainly in liver cells, and they are measured in units per liter (U/L).
Different laboratories can use slightly different reference ranges because their equipment and methods differ.
To convert total cholesterol from mg/dL to mmol/L, multiply by 0.0259.
Blood for most routine tests is drawn from a vein in the arm, and the sample is usually analyzed the same day.
An 'H' or 'L' next to a value simply means it is above or below that laboratory's reference range.
LDL is often calculated from the other lipid values rather than measured directly, which is one reason labs ask people to fast.
Some tests are timed around a medicine: for certain drug-level tests the sample is taken just before the next dose is due.
A urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio compares the amount of albumin to creatinine in a single urine sample.
Hematocrit is the percentage of blood volume made up of red blood cells.
Insulin is measured in units, which is why insulin pens and syringes are marked in units rather than milligrams.
A 'critical value' is a laboratory term for a result far enough outside the range that the lab phones the ordering clinician.
Hard exercise, dehydration and recent illness are examples of things that can shift a result for a short time.
Triglycerides are a type of fat carried in the blood, and levels rise for several hours after eating.
HDL is sometimes called 'good' cholesterol because it carries cholesterol away from the arteries.
Potassium is an electrolyte measured in mmol/L or mEq/L, and a sample that is handled roughly can give a falsely high reading.
High TSH levels can be seen in people with an underactive thyroid, among other causes.
Low ferritin may be associated with iron deficiency.
An elevated A1c is one of several findings clinicians use when assessing for diabetes.
Raised ALT can occur with fatty liver, viral hepatitis, alcohol use, or certain medicines.
A low eGFR is sometimes seen in chronic kidney disease, but a single value can also be affected by hydration and muscle mass.
Very high LDL from a young age is sometimes linked to an inherited condition called familial hypercholesterolemia.
Low vitamin B12 can be associated with certain diets, some medicines such as metformin, and conditions that affect absorption.
A high uric acid level is one of several possible reasons a clinician might look into gout, though many people with high levels never develop it.
Low hemoglobin is the laboratory finding that defines anemia in general, and anemia has many different causes.
In some people, a high white blood cell count reflects an infection; in others it follows stress, steroid medicines, or smoking.
Elevated triglycerides are commonly seen alongside insulin resistance, higher alcohol intake, or a non-fasting sample.
A positive ANA is found in a share of healthy adults as well as in people with autoimmune conditions.
High calcium may be related to the parathyroid glands, to supplements, or to other conditions.
Glucose values above the reference range can be seen in people with prediabetes or diabetes and also after a recent meal.
Low sodium can have many causes, including some diuretics and drinking very large amounts of water.
PSA can rise for reasons other than cancer, such as an enlarged prostate or a recent infection.
A low TSH can be seen in people with an overactive thyroid and in people taking thyroid hormone.
Protein in the urine may be associated with kidney conditions, but it can also appear temporarily after exercise or fever.
Raised creatinine does not have a single meaning: it may reflect kidney function, muscle mass, or certain medicines.
Mildly elevated bilirubin is often seen in people with Gilbert syndrome, a common and usually harmless inherited trait.
High blood pressure and diabetes are the two conditions most often linked with reduced kidney function in adults.
Low vitamin D levels are common in people who get little sun exposure and may be associated with weaker bones over time.
Statins are known to cause muscle aches in some people, and a CK test is one way clinicians look into that.
A high BNP can be seen in heart failure, and it also tends to be higher with age and with reduced kidney function.
Small red blood cells (a low MCV) are typically seen with iron deficiency or with inherited traits such as thalassemia.
Elevated platelets may follow inflammation, infection, or low iron, and less commonly reflect a bone marrow condition.
